title: Enlarged haemorrhoids: easing symptoms and checking bleeding
intro: Haemorrhoidal cushions are normal blood-vessel and supporting tissues inside the anal canal. When enlarged or displaced, they can cause bleeding, itching, mucus or a bulge. These symptoms are common and deserve care without embarrassment. However, finding haemorrhoids does not prove that every episode of rectal bleeding comes from them.

sections.heading: Understand the symptoms and other possible causes
paragraphs: Internal haemorrhoids may cause bright red bleeding or tissue that protrudes during a bowel movement. External lumps can have other causes, and a clot in an external haemorrhoid may be very painful. Severe pain is not something to assume is a routine internal haemorrhoid: a fissure, abscess or other condition may need different care. Tell the clinician about duration, amount and colour of blood, pain, bowel habits, mucus, medicines and previous treatment. Ongoing bleeding, a lasting change in stool pattern, unexplained weight loss or fatigue needs investigation rather than repeated creams. Even painless bleeding deserves medical advice.

sections.heading: Know when to seek urgent help
paragraphs: Continuous or heavy bleeding, large clots, fainting or major weakness requires emergency assessment. Black tarry stools or dark red bleeding needs urgent advice because the source may be elsewhere in the digestive tract. Fever, pus, rapidly increasing swelling or severe anal pain also needs prompt assessment. Mention anticoagulants and other medicines that affect bleeding; do not stop essential prescribed treatment on your own. The clinician may examine the anus and rectum, sometimes with a small viewing instrument, and decide whether further bowel investigation is needed. Ask for an explanation and chaperone and tell them if examination is too painful. Do not delay because you feel embarrassed.

sections.heading: Make stool easier to pass without straining
paragraphs: Gradually increase fibre if intake is low and drink an appropriate amount of fluid, respecting any medical fluid restriction. Whole grains, vegetables, fruit and pulses can help; a pharmacist or clinician may recommend a fibre supplement or suitable laxative if needed. Respond to the urge to pass stool, avoid forceful straining and do not sit on the toilet longer than necessary. Diarrhoea also needs attention rather than assuming only constipation matters. Gentle washing and patting dry can reduce irritation; avoid harsh rubbing or fragranced products. Activity as able and addressing medicines that cause constipation can support a practical plan. These measures help symptoms but do not replace assessment of bleeding.

sections.heading: Use symptom relief for a limited purpose
paragraphs: A pharmacist can advise short-term creams or suppositories for discomfort and itching, but these do not permanently remove large haemorrhoids. Follow the label and avoid prolonged unsupervised steroid or local anaesthetic use, which can irritate or damage skin. A comfortably warm bath or a wrapped cold pack may ease symptoms without burns or ice injury. Ask about appropriate pain relief; codeine can worsen constipation, and ibuprofen is not a good self-care choice when haemorrhoids are bleeding. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, other illnesses and medicines affect suitability. If symptoms fail to improve after a short trial, worsen or keep recurring, arrange a medical review rather than continuing products indefinitely. Never cut, puncture or band a lump yourself.

sections.heading: Procedures depend on the findings and impact
paragraphs: Persisting internal haemorrhoids may be treated with rubber-band ligation, injection treatment or another outpatient procedure. Larger prolapse, combined problems or failure of simpler treatment may lead to surgery. Choices differ in pain, recovery, recurrence and complications; the most extensive operation is not automatically best. Ask about your medicines, time off, bowel care, follow-up and urgent contacts before a procedure. A painful external clot may need a different discussion based on severity and timing. After treatment, increasing severe pain, fever, difficulty passing urine or substantial bleeding needs urgent assessment. Keep stool care going during recovery and ask when it is safe to return to usual activities.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: bleeding needs a fresh look
examples.text: Ana has previously been told she has haemorrhoids. When bleeding persists and her bowel pattern changes, she asks for reassessment instead of buying another cream. The clinician considers whether further investigation is needed even though haemorrhoids are present.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: making a procedure plan
examples.text: Ilir is offered banding for troublesome internal haemorrhoids. He asks about his regular medicines, expected discomfort, stool softening and warning symptoms. He knows that severe increasing pain or fever afterward is not something to simply wait out.
